---
title: "Quiz: from measurements to claims"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** You image 2000 cells from one treated dish and 2000 from one control dish, and a t-test on the cells gives $p = 10^{-12}$. What is $n$, and what can you conclude?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
At which level was the treatment applied independently?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$n = 1$ per condition: one dish each. The cells share their dish, so the test compares two dishes, and any difference between two dishes (seeding, medium, position in the incubator, imaging day) looks like a treatment effect. Nothing can be concluded about the treatment; repeat the experiment independently several times and compare the dish (or experiment) means.
:::

---

**Q2.** Explain a p-value of 0.03 in one sentence, without the word "probability of the hypothesis".

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Imagine the treatment does nothing.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
If the treatment had no effect, a difference at least as large as the observed one would come up by chance in about 3 % of repeated experiments.
:::

---

**Q3.** Why does measuring more cells per experiment hardly shrink the uncertainty of the treatment effect, while more experiments do?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which variation do the cells of one experiment share?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
All cells of one experiment share its day-to-day deviation. More cells average out the cell-to-cell variation but not that shared part; the uncertainty levels off at (day-to-day SD) × $\sqrt{2/E}$. Only more experiments average out the day-to-day variation.
:::

---

**Q4.** In a paired design, control and treated are done on the same day in each of 4 experiments. Why is this usually much more powerful than 4 control and 4 treated experiments on 8 different days?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What happens to the day effect in the difference?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Within each day, the day effect is the same for both conditions and cancels in the difference treated − control. The paired test compares differences that only contain the (smaller) within-day variation; the unpaired test has to see the effect through the large day-to-day variation.
:::

---

**Q5.** You measure 500 features and report the 12 with $p < 0.05$ as "affected by the treatment". What is the problem, and what would you do?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How many hits would chance give?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
With no real effect at all, $0.05 \cdot 500 = 25$ features would be expected below 0.05; 12 hits are fully compatible with no effect. Correct for multiple testing: Benjamini–Hochberg to control the share of false discoveries, or Bonferroni ($p \le 0.0001$) to control the chance of any false hit; and confirm the hits in a new experiment.
:::

---

**Q6.** All control wells were imaged on Monday and all treated wells on Tuesday. A colleague suggests a mixed-effects model with day as a random effect. Will it help?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Can any analysis separate the day from the treatment here?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No. Day and treatment are confounded: every difference between the conditions is also a difference between the days, and no model can split it. Only the design can: both conditions on every day (and every plate), randomised positions.
:::

---

**Q7.** Report A: "p < 0.001". Report B: "the area increased by 9 % (95 % CI 2 to 16 %), n = 5 experiments". Why is B more useful?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What do you want to know about an effect?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
B gives the size of the effect, its uncertainty, and the unit of replication with its $n$; the reader can judge whether 2–16 % matters biologically. A p-value alone says neither how large the effect is nor whether $n$ counted cells or experiments; with enough cells any tiny difference gives $p < 0.001$.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Cells within an experiment have intra-class correlation $\rho = 0.1$. What is the design effect for 100 cells per experiment, and what is the false-positive rate of a cells-as-$n$ z-test at 5 %?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Design effect $1 + (m-1)\rho$; the z statistic has that variance instead of 1.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$1 + 99 \cdot 0.1 = 10.9$. The z statistic has SD $\sqrt{10.9} = 3.30$, so $P(|z| > 1.96) = 2\Phi(-1.96/3.30) = 2\Phi(-0.59) = 0.55$: 55 % false positives instead of 5 %.
:::
